listing_view.reasoning: Subscription ramped from ~0.44x to ~2.9x by day two [demand figures], which is decent but not exceptional momentum for a mainboard IPO, and we have no GMP or anchor data to confirm institutional appetite. A ~13.7x P/E against a stated 18.31x benchmark gives some pricing headroom, but the negative latest-year operating cash flow is exactly the kind of flag that can cap aftermarket sentiment once noticed.

longterm_view.reasoning: Revenue compounding near 29% with PAT margins recovering to ~9.6% and an order book of ₹12,047mn (~2.7x latest revenue) supports multi-year growth visibility [business, page 245]. The offsetting concerns are real: ROCE has fallen from 47.5% to 28.8%, the latest year converted zero profit into cash (OCF -₹121mn), and debt rose even as net worth doubled — growth is being bought, not self-funded.

governance.reasoning: The document's printed debt-to-equity of 0.23 cannot be reproduced from its own balance sheet (our computation gives ~1.18), which is a serious internal-consistency red flag in a seller-prepared document. Related-party disclosures and director guarantees secured personally [promoters, page 358; promoters, page 432] are ordinary but add to related-party exposure we cannot fully size from these extracts.

key_risks.risk: Negative operating cash flow in the latest year
key_risks.why_it_matters: Reported PAT of ₹432.9mn arrived as -₹121mn of operating cash, meaning earnings quality is unproven and growth depends on external funding.
The printed 0.23 debt-to-equity is irreconcilable with the document's own borrowings and net worth, undermining reliance on other stated ratios.
ROCE falling from 47.5% to 28.8% over three years suggests each new rupee deployed earns less, so the growth story may be diluting quality.
The company itself flags that future business procurement is becoming more uncertain, which directly threatens the order-book-led growth thesis.
Inability to recover additional expenses or manage time overruns would hit margins in what appears to be a project/contract business.

answers.question: where did the money go — receivables, inventory, or both?
answers.answer: It did not go into receivables: receivable days collapsed from 94 to 19.5, so customers are paying far faster than two years ago. The negative latest-year operating cash flow therefore points to inventory and/or project work-in-progress and advances absorbing cash, consistent with a swelling order book [business, page 245]. But the extracts contain no inventory line, so I cannot prove the split — 'not receivables' is established; 'inventory specifically' is inference, not evidence.
answers.citation: balance sheet and cash verified figures; inventory split not answerable from what I was given

answer.what_would_change_my_mind: A reconciliation of the debt-to-equity discrepancy and a cash-flow breakdown showing the negative OCF was one-off project build (not structural) would move me materially higher on the long-term view; conversely, evidence the fresh-issue proceeds mainly repay promoter-linked debt would push me lower.
